audioScript: Moving out of the dorm turned out to be a piece of cake.

choices.text: I'd like a piece of chocolate cake.
The dorm moved its mailroom last year.
Lucky you. It took me an entire weekend.
I'm moving to a new seat in class.

explanation: The key reacts to the idiom meaning very easy, while "I'd like a piece of chocolate cake" takes the idiom literally.

audioScript: I'm not sure the twenty-four-hour study lounge was worth giving up the game room.

choices.text: Twenty-four students signed up for the trip.
The lounge is on the fourth floor.
I gave my old board games to my brother.
Well, it's packed every night, so people use it.

explanation: The key offers evidence against the speaker's doubt, while "Twenty-four students signed up for the trip" only repeats the number.

audioScript: I hate to ask, but could I borrow your car to move a couch this weekend?

choices.text: I'd help, but a couch won't fit in my compact.
I hate waiting in long lines at the store too.
The couch in the lounge is really comfortable.
I borrowed a book from the library yesterday.

explanation: The key politely refuses with a practical reason, while "I borrowed a book from the library" echoes borrow but answers nothing.

audioScript: Why does the café always run out of oat milk by noon?

choices.text: It runs from seven until three on weekdays.
I'd guess they only get one delivery a week.
Noon is when I usually eat lunch.
I actually prefer almond milk in my coffee.

explanation: The key offers a plausible reason, while "It runs from seven until three on weekdays" echoes run and answers until when.

audioScript: The trainer said I need to cut back on lifting until my shoulder heals.

choices.text: I cut my hair shorter last week.
The trainer drives a blue truck.
My shoulder bag is really heavy with books today.
Makes sense. Maybe swimming would be easier on it.

explanation: The key accepts the advice and suggests an alternative, while "I cut my hair shorter last week" plays on the phrasal verb cut back.

audioScript: The heat in our building is on full blast, and it's sixty degrees outside.

choices.text: I had a blast at the concert.
Let's report it. They can probably adjust the boiler.
The building has about sixty rooms on four floors.
It's supposed to rain outside later.

explanation: The key proposes a fix for the overheating, while "I had a blast at the concert" uses blast in an idiom with a different meaning.

audioScript: Is it worth getting the unlimited meal plan if I usually skip breakfast?

choices.text: I skipped class once to finish my paper.
The plan was announced at orientation.
It was definitely worth the trip downtown.
Probably not. The ten-meal plan would save you money.

explanation: The key gives a recommendation with a reason, while "It was definitely worth the trip downtown" echoes worth about something else.

audioScript: The rec center is offering free swimming lessons to beginners all semester.

choices.text: Perfect timing. I never learned how to swim.
I'm offering my old bike for sale.
I began a new novel yesterday.
The semester ends in mid-December.

explanation: The key reacts with personal relevance, while "I began a new novel yesterday" is a sound-alike trap on beginners.

audioScript: I'm locked out, and the front desk doesn't open for another hour.

choices.text: I locked my bike outside the library this morning.
The front desk handles packages too.
You're welcome to wait in my room until then.
Another hour of studying, then dinner.

explanation: The key offers practical help for the implied problem, while "I locked my bike outside the library" echoes locked.

audioScript: I'd say living off campus is cheaper once you factor in the meal plan.

choices.text: Factor the numbers and divide by two.
Maybe, but you'd also pay for transportation.
The meal was cheaper than I expected.
I live about two blocks from campus.

explanation: The key responds to the opinion with a counterpoint, while "Factor the numbers and divide by two" takes factor in its math sense.

audioScript: I thought you'd quit the swim team after the first month.

choices.text: Swimming is good for your back.
I quit drinking soda in January.
I almost did, but the coach talked me into staying.
The team won its very first meet last month.

explanation: The key explains why the speaker's assumption is wrong, while "I quit drinking soda in January" echoes quit about something else.

audioScript: When you get a chance, could you take a look at the sink in room three-twelve?

choices.text: Chances are it'll rain again tomorrow afternoon.
I'm on another call, but I'll come by after lunch.
Room three-twelve is on the third floor, I think.
I already looked at the lunch menu, thanks.

explanation: The key agrees and gives a realistic time, while "Room three-twelve is on the third floor" only gives the location.

audioScript: With finals coming up, the gym is the last place I want to be.

choices.text: Even a short workout might help you clear your head.
Finals are in the main lecture hall.
I want to be a personal trainer.
The last place I lived had a gym downstairs.

explanation: The key responds to the speaker's reluctance with encouragement, while "The last place I lived had a gym" takes the last place literally.

audioScript: Why don't you join our study group in the dorm lounge tonight?

choices.text: Tonight's dinner is lasagna, I heard.
Thanks, but I'm covering a shift at the café.
We joined that same group last spring, actually.
The lounge closes at midnight, I think.

explanation: The key politely declines with a reason, while "The lounge closes at midnight, I think" echoes lounge and does not accept or decline.

audioScript: How am I supposed to sleep with the construction crew starting at six every morning?

choices.text: Six people work on that crew.
They're building a new parking garage.
Have you tried earplugs? The front desk has them.
I slept right through my alarm yesterday morning.

explanation: The key answers the frustrated question with a practical solution, while "I slept right through my alarm yesterday morning" echoes sleep without helping.

audioScript: The line for the yoga class wraps all the way around the building.

choices.text: The building was designed in the sixties.
Then let's skip it and go running.
Yoga helps me relax before exams.
I wrapped the gift last night.

explanation: The key infers the class is too crowded and suggests an alternative, while "I wrapped the gift last night" echoes wraps literally.
